costGuide.title: BMW S63TU Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting an S63TU typically takes 18-24 hours at £80-£120/hr (independent M specialist) - the hot‑vee configuration, twin turbos, Valvetronic system, and complex cooling make this one of BMW's most labour‑intensive engine swaps.
paragraphs: The biggest price movers for an S63TU replacement are the variant (TU, TU2, TU3, TU4 - later variants with higher output and improved cooling command a premium), turbocharger condition (OEM replacements are £2,500+ each), and whether the engine is from a standard M car or an Alpina‑spec unit. The TU3 and TU4 variants feature different pistons, higher fuel pressure, and revised cooling - these are more expensive to source and rebuild. failures.title: BMW S63TU Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Valve Stem Seal Wear (Improved but Not Eliminated)
items.whatHappens: The S63TU introduced improved valve stem seals and better oil separation compared to the original S63B44A, but the hot‑vee design still generates significant heat that eventually degrades the seals. Symptoms include blue smoke on startup (especially after idling), increased oil consumption, and fouled spark plugs - though less severe than on the pre‑TU engine.
items.repairVsReplace: Valve stem seal replacement is a major job (£2,000-£4,000) requiring cylinder head removal. If caught early, the engine can be saved. If ignored, oil consumption can lead to catalytic converter failure. Read our full /failures/valve-stem-seal-failure guide

items.title: Turbocharger Coolant and Oil Line Leaks
items.whatHappens: The S63TU's twin turbochargers are mounted in the hot‑vee, with coolant and oil lines that can become brittle and leak over time. Coolant leaks can lead to overheating; oil leaks can cause turbocharger bearing failure. The integrated coolant lines on the turbocharger housings are a known weak point.
items.repairVsReplace: Line replacement is possible (£800-£1,500) but if the turbochargers have suffered oil starvation, replacement (£2,500-£4,000 per turbo) is required.

items.title: Oil Leaks - valve covers and oil filter housing
items.whatHappens: Like the pre‑TU S63, the S63TU suffers from valve cover gasket and oil filter housing gasket leaks as the high operating temperatures cause gaskets to harden. Oil leaks can lead to low oil levels, which on a high‑performance V8 with twin turbos is a serious risk.
items.repairVsReplace: Gasket replacement is labour‑intensive but manageable for an M specialist. However, if oil starvation has occurred, bearing damage may have already taken place - in which case a replacement unit is recommended.

items.title: Fuel Injector and HPFP Issues
items.whatHappens: The S63TU's direct injection system operates at high pressure (up to 350 bar on later variants). Injectors can become clogged or fail, leading to rough idle, misfires, and reduced power. High‑pressure fuel pump (HPFP) failure is also reported on higher‑mileage examples.
items.repairVsReplace: Injector replacement (£200-£500 each) is a specialist job. HPFP replacement costs £800-£1,500.

failures.goodYearsLine: The S63TU is a significant improvement over the original S63B44A - Valvetronic, higher compression (10.0:1), improved oil separation, and revised cooling make it more durable. The later TU3 (2020+) and TU4 variants introduced further improvements including higher fuel pressure, revised pistons, and strengthened bottom ends. The S63TU is considered reliable for a high‑performance V8, with many F10 M5 owners reporting 100,000+ trouble‑free miles with diligent maintenance. The 2017+ F90 M5's engine benefits from further cooling and oil system improvements.

variants.title: S63TU Sub‑Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: INTRO: The S63TU (Technical Update) covers several sub‑codes that represent successive generations of BMW M's twin‑turbo V8. Unlike the original S63B44A (which lacked Valvetronic), all S63TU engines feature variable valve timing, but each sub‑code brings unique improvements in power output, fuel pressure, and durability. Understanding which sub‑code you have is essential when sourcing a replacement - fitting the wrong generation without the corresponding ECU and cooling system changes will not work. - Fitted to: F10 M5 (2013-2016), F12/F13 M6 (2013-2018), F85 X5 M (2015-2019), F86 X6 M (2015-2019) - Key technical difference: First S63 with Valvetronic variable valve timing. Introduces improved oil separation and revised cooling over the pre‑TU S63B44A. Compression ratio increased to 10.0:1 (from 9.3:1 on the S63B44A). - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above - valve stem seals, turbo lines, oil leaks. The S63B44B is considered significantly more reliable than the S63B44A, but the valve stem seal issue persists on higher‑mileage examples. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with any S63TU3 or TU4 engine - the ECU calibration, fuel system, and cooling system architecture differ. The S63B44B uses a different injector design and lower fuel pressure than later variants. - Fitted to: F90 M5 (2017-2018), F90 M5 Competition (2018-2023) - Key technical difference: Revised pistons, higher fuel pressure, and improved cooling over the B variant. Introduces a revised oil pump design and updated ECU calibration. 600 hp in base tune, 617 hp in Competition form. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern - improved valve stem seals over earlier TU variants, but still a known wear point. Cooling system improvements reduce heat‑related wear. - Interchange note: Not a direct swap with the S63B44B - the T0 engine has different ECU hardware, wiring, and cooling system connections. Fitting a T0 into an F10 M5 requires significant modification. - Fitted to: F90 M5 Competition (2018-2023), F92/F93 M8 (2019-2021) - Key technical difference: Higher boost pressure and revised ECU calibration over the T0 variant. Different cooling system architecture to handle sustained track use. Same hardware as T0 but with different mapping. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares family pattern. T1‑spec engines are found in Competition models and are generally well‑supported for track use. - Interchange note: The T1 is mechanically identical to the T0 but with different ECU calibration - interchange is possible with proper ECU reflashing. - Fitted to: F95 X5 M Competition, F96 X6 M Competition (2020-present) - Key technical difference: Further revised internals, higher fuel pressure (350 bar), and upgraded cooling. Features the latest oil pump and bearing designs for SUV applications. 625 hp output. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares family pattern. The T2 is the most robust S63 variant for high‑stress SUV applications. - Interchange note: Not a direct swap with earlier TU variants - the T2 uses different engine mounts, cooling system layout, and transmission mating. - Fitted to: F90 M5 CS (2022-2023) - Key technical difference: Ultimate S63TU variant. 635 hp from a track‑focused calibration, with unique camshaft profiles, lightweight internals, and bespoke cooling. Significantly lower production volume than other variants. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares family pattern but CS‑spec engines are typically maintained to a higher standard due to vehicle value. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with any other variant - unique ECU calibration and bespoke internals make this a specialist‑only replacement. - Fitted to: Later production F95 X5 M, F96 X6 M, F92 M8 Competition (2022-present) - Key technical difference: Latest evolution with further cooling and emissions improvements. Incorporates lessons from the M5 CS cooling system design. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Too early in lifecycle to have widespread documented failures; shares family pattern. - Interchange note: The T4 is the most current S63 variant - sourcing a replacement is possible but expensive (£14,000+). How to confirm your code: The engine code is stamped on a machined pad on the left‑hand side of the engine block (viewed from the front) and appears on the V5C under "Engine number" - the code will read S63B44Bxxxxxx, S63B44T0xxxxxx, S63B44T1xxxxxx, S63B44T2xxxxxx, S63B44T3xxxxxx, or S63B44T4xxxxxx. Alternatively, use a BMW VIN decoder to extract the exact engine code from your vehicle's build sheet.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement S63TU - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used S63TU can make financial sense only if it comes from a low‑mileage, well‑documented donor with proof of regular oil changes and cooling system maintenance. Given the engine's known weaknesses (valve stem seals, turbocharger lines, oil leaks), a used unit without history is a high‑risk purchase - the cost of addressing these issues on a used engine can quickly exceed the purchase price. Used prices from £5,500-£9,000 reflect this risk. Always check which TU variant you're buying - a T0/T1 from an F90 M5 is not a straight fit for an F10 M5. Link once:

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A properly reconditioned S63TU is the recommended choice for most owners. A full recon should address the engine's known weak points: new valve stem seals, turbocharger inspection/rebuild, new water pump and thermostat, full gasket set, and timing chain inspection. Given the £9,000-£14,000 supply cost and the host vehicle value (£15,000-£80,000+ depending on variant), this is the best balance of cost and reliability. A 12-24 month warranty is essential on an engine of this complexity. Link once:

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full S63TU rebuild is justified for low‑mileage, high‑value examples (F90 M5 CS, M8 Competition) or where the owner plans significant tuning. An upgraded rebuild should include forged pistons, upgraded rod bearings, improved oil pump, and upgraded turbochargers. Rebuild costs (£12,000-£18,000+) are significant but still well below a new OEM crate engine from BMW (estimated £20,000-£25,000+). Only M‑specialist workshops with S63TU experience should be trusted. Link once:

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: All supply options can be fitted through our network of vetted BMW M specialists nationwide, with a minimum 12‑month warranty on reconditioned and rebuilt units and full nationwide delivery coverage. Link once:
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The S63TU sits in high‑value M vehicles ranging from £15,000-£25,000 (F10 M5, F12 M6) to £30,000-£80,000+ (F90 M5, X5 M, M8) [THIRD‑PARTY - AutoTrader UK market data 2025]. A £9,000-£14,000 reconditioned unit represents 15-60% of the vehicle's value on older examples - on a £15,000 F10 M5, a £9,000 replacement is 60% of the vehicle's value, making it a borderline financial decision. On an F90 M5 or X5 M, the higher retained value comfortably absorbs the replacement cost. For F10 M5 and F12 M6 owners: if your S63TU has suffered catastrophic failure and your vehicle is worth under £18,000, evaluate scrap or part‑exchange value before committing to a replacement. These are enthusiast vehicles - some owners will justify the spend regardless of market value, but the honest marketplace‑neutrality position is that a £9,000+ engine in a sub‑£18,000 car requires serious thought.

items.question: What is the most common failure on the BMW S63TU?
items.answer: Valve stem seal wear remains the most common issue, though less severe than on the pre‑TU S63B44A. Typical onset is 80,000-120,000 miles. Symptoms include blue smoke on startup and increased oil consumption. Turbocharger coolant and oil line leaks are also common, as are oil leaks from valve cover gaskets. Fuel injector and high‑pressure fuel pump failure occurs on higher‑mileage examples. The S63TU introduced Valvetronic, higher compression (10.0:1), and improved oil separation - all addressing S63B44A weaknesses. Later variants (T0, T1, T2, T3, T4) feature further improvements.

items.answer: The engine code is stamped on a machined pad on the left‑hand side of the engine block (viewed from the front) and appears on the V5C under 'Engine number' - the code will read S63B44Bxxxxxx, S63B44T0xxxxxx, S63B44T1xxxxxx, S63B44T2xxxxxx, S63B44T3xxxxxx, or S63B44T4xxxxxx. Use a BMW VIN decoder to confirm from the build sheet. S63B44B = 553-575 hp (F10 M5, F12 M6, F85 X5 M, F86 X6 M). S63B44T0 = 600-617 hp (F90 M5, F92 M8). S63B44T1 = 617 hp (F90 M5 Competition, F92 M8 Competition). S63B44T2 = 625 hp (F95 X5 M, F96 X6 M Competition). S63B44T3 = 635 hp (F90 M5 CS). S63B44T4 = 625-635 hp (latest F95/F96/F92).

items.question: Is the S63TU reliable, and what mileage can I expect?
items.answer: The S63TU is considered a significant reliability improvement over the S63B44A. With diligent maintenance - 5,000‑mile oil changes, proactive cooling system care, and early attention to valve stem seals - many engines reach 120,000-150,000 miles before needing major work. The later T0-T4 variants are even more robust, with F90 M5 owners reporting 80,000+ trouble‑free miles regularly. Budget for valve stem seal replacement around 80,000-100,000 miles as preventative maintenance. Replace water pump and thermostat at 60,000-80,000 miles. Full service history is non‑negotiable - this engine requires careful maintenance. The S63TU is considered more reliable than the Audi 4.0 TFSI and Mercedes‑AMG M177 in comparable tuning levels.
